lesson.title: Why Atoms Bother Sticking Together
lesson.summary: A chemical bond forms whenever atoms can lower their overall potential energy by sharing, transferring, or pooling valence electrons, the single organizing idea behind ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding.
lesson.body:
Atoms bond for a simple reason: the resulting arrangement of nuclei and electrons has lower total energy than the separate atoms did on their own. Isolated atoms, except for the noble gases, are relatively high energy, unstable arrangements, because their valence shells are incomplete. When two atoms come close enough that their valence electrons can rearrange, whether by transferring fully from one atom to the other or by being shared between them, the system can reach a lower energy, more stable configuration. That drop in potential energy is released, usually as heat, so bond formation is exothermic. This is why chemical bonds connect so directly to two more fundamental ideas: valence electrons, which are the electrons actually involved in bonding, and energy, since the whole reason bonding happens at all is that it lowers the system's energy.

The clearest way to see this is to picture two atoms approaching each other from far apart. At a large distance, there is essentially no interaction and the potential energy is close to zero. As the atoms get closer, the attraction between one atom's nucleus and the other atom's electrons begins to pull them together, and the potential energy decreases. If the atoms keep approaching, though, the two positively charged nuclei begin to repel each other, and at very short distances that repulsion dominates and the energy rises sharply. Somewhere in between lies a minimum, an optimal bond length where the attractive and repulsive forces balance. That minimum is the actual bond that forms, and the depth of that energy well, how far potential energy drops below zero, is the bond energy: the amount of energy that must be added to pull the bonded atoms back apart.

Chemists sort bonds into three broad categories based on how the valence electrons are handled, and each category gets its own detailed treatment. Ionic bonds form when one atom's valence electrons are essentially transferred to another atom, typically between a metal with a low ionization energy and a nonmetal with a strongly negative electron affinity, producing oppositely charged ions that attract each other electrostatically. Covalent bonds form when two atoms, usually both nonmetals, share one or more pairs of valence electrons rather than transferring them outright, with the shared pair occupying the space between both nuclei. Metallic bonds form among metal atoms, where valence electrons are not tied to any single atom or pair of atoms but instead spread out across the entire sample as a shared, mobile electron sea.

What unites all three categories is that the driving force is always the same: incomplete valence shells represent higher energy, less stable arrangements, and bonding is simply the process by which atoms rearrange their valence electrons to reach a lower energy, more stable state, often one that resembles the full valence shell of the nearest noble gas. Which specific type of bond forms in a given case depends mostly on how the atoms involved compare in electronegativity and how many valence electrons each one has to offer or needs to receive, a relationship that becomes the focus of the ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding topics that follow. Chemical bonds are, at their core, the answer to a question posed by energy itself: can this collection of atoms find a lower energy way to arrange its valence electrons than it had while separate?
